questions.lessonTitle: The Two Approaches to Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to shrinking image file sizes. The first approach involves throwing away parts of the image data that humans won't notice, which is called lossy compression. The second approach involves being clever about how every pixel is stored while preserving all original data, which is called lossless compression. These two approaches form the foundation of all image compression techniques used today. Lossy compression is used by formats like JPEG, while lossless compression is used by formats like PNG. Both approaches address the same core problem: reducing the 6.2 MB raw size of an HD image to something more manageable.

Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values, reducing the overall bit count.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that humans won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering or prediction to shrink file size by storing differences between adjacent pixels rather than actual values. Instead of storing each value directly, PNG predicts each pixel's value based on its neighbors and stores only how wrong that prediction was. PNG supports four prediction methods that encoders try per row, selecting whichever compresses best. The Sub method predicts from the left neighbor and works best for horizontal gradients. The Up method predicts from the pixel above and works best for vertical gradients. The Average method predicts from the average of left and above pixels. The Paeth method smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal neighbors.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering, PNG uses an algorithm called LZ77 to find patterns in the data. LZ77 works by spotting repeated sequences and replacing them with back-references instead of storing the same values twice. Instead of repeating a sequence, LZ77 says "go back X values and copy Y" - this tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the actual values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data that it scans for patterns. Any repeated pattern within that 32 KB window can be referenced instead of being stored again, significantly reducing file size for images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients.
questions.question: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering and pattern-finding, PNG uses Huffman coding to give common values shorter binary codes. Some values appear much more frequently than others in the filtered data. The value 0 (representing no difference from prediction) might appear 60% of the time, while 127 might appear only 5% of the time. With Huffman coding, common values get shorter bit representations: 0 appears 60% and gets just 1 bit (0), 2 appears 25% and gets 2 bits (10), 255 appears 10% and gets 3 bits (110), and 127 appears 5% and gets 3 bits (111). This mathematical arrangement results in files that are approximately 5x smaller than storing every value in 8 bits.

questions.explanation: The value 0, which appears 60% of the time, receives the shortest code (1 bit: 0). This is because Huffman coding gives shorter codes to more frequently occurring values.

questions.lessonTitle: PNG Lossless Compression: Filter Prediction Process

The Sub filter predicts each pixel based on the left neighbor (best for horizontal gradients). The Up filter predicts based on the pixel above (best for vertical gradients). The Average filter uses the average of left and above. The Paeth filter smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal. The encoder tests all four methods, selects the one that compresses best, then applies that method to the row.

choices: Apply the selected filter to the row

questions.lessonTitle: The Three Tricks of PNG Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression used by PNG preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file size. It uses three distinct tricks to achieve this compression. Trick 1 is filtering or prediction, where instead of storing each pixel value directly, we store how much each pixel differs from its neighbor since adjacent pixels are usually similar. Trick 2 is LZ77, which finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with back-references like "go back 5 values and copy 5" instead of repeating the values. Trick 3 is Huffman coding, which gives common values shorter binary codes while giving rare values longer codes.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG and the Three Tricks
questions.lessonContent: PNG supports four distinct prediction methods that determine how each pixel is compared to its neighbors. The Sub method predicts each pixel from its left neighbor, which works best for horizontal gradients. The Up method predicts from the pixel directly above, best for vertical gradients. The Average method predicts from the average of the left and above pixels. The Paeth method is the most sophisticated, as it intelligently chooses between the left, above, or diagonal pixel based on which is closest. PNG encoders actually try each method for every row and automatically select the one that produces the best compression for that specific row.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG and the Three Tricks
questions.lessonContent: After the filtering step transforms pixel data into differences, the LZ77 algorithm searches for repeated patterns within the filtered data. It maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data it has processed. When LZ77 finds a sequence that matches something earlier in this window, it replaces the repeated sequence with a back-reference. For example, instead of storing the sequence "0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2" repeatedly, it might say "go back 5 values and copy 5" - this tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the actual values. This technique is particularly effective for images with large solid color regions or gradual gradients.

Each of these color values ranges from 0, which means none of that color, to 255, which represents the maximum intensity of that color. questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Introduction to Image Compression and Digital Images
questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to compressing image files to make them smaller. The first approach is called lossy compression, which throws away parts of the image data that humans are unlikely to notice, trading some quality for significantly smaller file sizes. The second approach is called lossless compression, which uses clever techniques to store every single pixel perfectly while still achieving some size reduction. These two ideas form the foundation for all major image formats used today, including JPEG (which uses lossy compression) and PNG (which uses lossless compression). The choice between them depends on the use case: photographs typically use lossy compression for efficiency, while screenshots and graphics with sharp edges benefit from lossless compression to preserve every detail.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Lossless Compression and File Formats
questions.lessonContent: The PNG file format wraps compressed data in a structured organization of chunks, each serving a specific purpose. A PNG file begins with a signature (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A in hexadecimal), followed by required chunks including IHDR (the Image Header containing metadata such as width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (the actual image data), and IEND (the end marker). Each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum at the end, which is a mathematical fingerprint of its data. When you open a PNG file, your computer recalculates this fingerprint and compares it to the stored value; if they don't match, the file is detected as damaged or corrupted. This checksum system protects against issues like bad network connections or buggy programs.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Lossless Compression and File Formats
questions.lessonContent: The PNG format combines three compression techniques in sequence to achieve lossless compression. First, filtering stores pixel differences rather than absolute values, making the data more compressible. Second, LZ77 algorithm scans for repeated patterns within a sliding window of the last 32 KB and replaces them with back-references (e.g., 'go back 5 values and copy 5'). Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, where the value 0 appearing 60% of the time gets just 1 bit while rarer values get more bits. This pipeline typically achieves 3x compression for photographs (6.2 MB to ~2.1 MB) and 10-50x compression for screenshots with large solid color regions. The same combination of LZ77 and Huffman also powers ZIP files and web traffic compression (gzip/Brotli).

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression uses three main techniques to shrink files while preserving all data. Trick 1 is filtering or prediction: instead of storing actual pixel values, the algorithm stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor (like predicting from the left, above, or averaging both).
